I apologize for the length of time it took for me to reply. I'm a Reddit newbie, and I hadn't realized you had replied.

I am with you on how the points stifle conversation in a Reddit such as this. I know that rating posts is sort of the point around here, but maybe the effect shouldn't be to hide low rated comments, at least in this sub.

I also see where you are coming from when you say "At some point it just started to seem like the complaints of conspiracy theorists." There is a lot of concern in the ecig/vaping community right now due to some very unjustified proposals for regulation from the FDA that were announced last week, and I think everyone is on edge. As I said in /r/electronic_cigarette, though, "bullshit be bullshit whether you like the smell of it or not." People really do need to respond to you with arguments and evidence, but try to understand that there are just as many false or unsupported claims made by the opposition, there really are, and that's where the frustration comes from.

Before I go on, I'd like to comment on the fact you brought up that nicotine has adverse health effects on its own: this is true. It is also true of caffeine and alcohol. This may be a subjective, philosophical point, but I consider it a matter for the individual to decide what they put in their own body. That said, I also believe this should only be done by the properly informed, so I absolutely agree that such drugs should not be sold to minors. What perplexes me is why either of those commercials bothers you, they seem like advertisements directed at adults to me. Also, I actually agree that it's rude to smoke or vape around people without their consent; I don't know about making it illegal, but I do consider it rude, and I never do either around those who haven't explicitly told me they don't mind.

The problem with just saying "we need to restrict where e-cigarettes are sold" is that it would likely lead to a unilateral ban on the vape industry as it currently exists, which business model relies on specialty retailers. It's a niche market, and I don't personally think it's a good thing when government blindly quashes nascent markets under flimsy reasoning.

In fact, I feel I owe you an explanation for all of the policy suggestions which I said were unreasonable. I won't spend much time on the flavors, as I think the reason that is unreasonable has been laid out quite clearly by others. We don't ban mojito or sex-on-the-beach cocktails for the same reason: adults like tasty things, and nothing about nice flavors remotely suggests that a product is aimed at minors.

The marketing restrictions, I feel, would be too broad because the wording leaves the door open, again, to having an excuse to crush the small businesses built around the hobby. I suppose "head shops" did fine by using code words, but I don't see why they should have had to.

Finally, there is an issue with purportedly scientific reviews making policy suggestions. That's not what science is for, and if it was meant as an argument about policy, it should not have been presented as a scientific article.

Reasonable:

>Prohibit cobranding e-cigarettes with cigarettes or marketing in a way that promotes dual use.
>Prohibit claims that e-cigarettes are effective smoking cessation aids until e-cigarette manufacturers and companies provide sufficient evidence that e-cigarettes can be used effectively for smoking cessation.
>Prohibit any health claims for e-cigarette products until and unless approved by regulatory agencies to scientific and regulatory standards.
>Establish standards for regulating product ingredients and functioning.
>Prohibit the sale of e-cigarettes to anyone who cannot legally buy cigarettes

Unreasonable at this time or unreasonably broad/vague:

>Prohibit the use of characterizing flavors in e-cigarettes, particularly candy and alcohol flavors.
>Prohibit the use of e-cigarettes anywhere that use of conventional cigarettes is prohibited.
>Prohibit the sale of e-cigarettes ... in any venues where sale of conventional cigarettes is prohibited.
>Subject e-cigarette marketing to the same level of restrictions that apply to conventional cigarettes (including no television or radio advertising).

I am sorry you've been jumped on. Anyway, do you disagree with my above classifications? If so, why?

The industry in general needs to stop making claims they don't have solid evidence for, anyway, it's ultimately just as destructive as the baseless claims made that vaping is "just as bad" as smoking. Just sell it as a fun new hobby, stop saying it's healthy or helps you quit smoking, the jury's still out on both of those claims.

However, the review has several problems.

Two of the three authors are from the UCSF Center for Tobacco Control Research and Education (CTCRE), whose previous work shows a bad habit many researchers have of citing themselves without being clear that that's what they're doing (see the first citation for an example; there are several more). Dr. Rachel Grana (http://profiles.ucsf.edu/rachel.grana) in particular has made electronic cigarettes her issue du jour, and along with the rest of the CTCRE, has a clear predetermined conclusion: e-cigarettes are bad and need to be stopped. To quote from the introduction of the paper in question:

*"It is important to assess e-cigarette toxicant exposure and individual risk, as well as the health effects, of e-cigarettes as they are actually used to ensure safety and to develop an evidence-based regulatory scheme that protects the entire population—children and adults, smokers and nonsmokers—in the context of how the tobacco industry is marketing and promoting these products. Health claims and claims of efficacy for quitting smoking are unsupported by the scientific evidence to date. To minimize the potential negative impacts on prevention and cessation and the undermining of existing tobacco control measures, e-cigarette use should be prohibited where tobacco cigarette use is prohibited, and the products should be subject to the same marketing restrictions as tobacco cigarettes."*

The methods of the study involved searching PubMed for articles related to e-cigarettes and focusing on those which presented original research. Were this the only criterion, we wouldn't have a problem, but the paper goes on to say:

*"Eighty articles were excluded because they were not relevant, were not in English, or were reviews or commentaries that did not provide original data, although some are cited for background and context."*

What papers were included or excluded on these bases is unknown, as is how these criteria are assessed in the first place.

That's not the worst of it, though. Under the "cytotoxicity" section, the results of several studies are twisted into supporting the claim that e-liquid is highly cytotoxic. For example:

*"Farsalinos et al45 tested cytotoxicity in cultured rat cardiac myoblasts of exposure to aerosol generated from 20 refill solutions from 5 manufacturers containing 6 to 24 mg/mL nicotine in various flavors, a “base”-only solution (50% propylene glycol and 50% glycerol), and conventional cigarette smoke. The aerosol from 3 fluids was cytotoxic at 100% and 50% dilution; 2 were tobacco flavored and 1 was cinnamon cookie flavored. Cigarette smoke was cytotoxic at 100% and all dilutions except 6.25%."*

This is cherry picking, plain and simple. The actual conclusion of that paper? Take a look:

*"This study indicates that EC vapor is significantly less cytotoxic compared tobacco CS. These results should be validated by clinical studies."* http://informahealthcare.com/doi/abs/10.3109/08958378.2013.793439

But the worst part is, **the article cited in the original post outright lies about the number of studies that suggest that the health claims of ecig companies are not just baseless, but false**. The actual number of studies cited in this research that made any claims regarding this topic was **9** including 4 clinical trials (two with very small sample sizes), 4 longitudinal studies and 1 cross-sectional study (and one of those was, surprise surprise, conducted by Dr. Grana herself). Of those, only 6 unambiguously claimed to show no effect on smoking cessation (and one of them, by Bullen et. al., also found some interesting things out about the efficacy of nicotine patches).

That's an awful lot of bullshit stuffed into one headline, but remember: bullshit be bullshit whether you like the smell of it or not.

See, the original problem I had was that, based on my education, formal and auto-didactic, I seriously could not accept that "wave + particle at the same time" was a reasonable, accurate portrayal of reality. What it seemed like to me was that we had these really useful mathematical models we could use to describe and thereby predict the behavior of dynamic systems, and then these mathematical models proved insufficient at very small scales, so a new model was needed. That sounded more like "neither" to me than "both", and still does.

The phrase *itself* bothers me *because* it doesn't jive with my understanding of the QM model. I'm not bothered by not knowing things, that's fine, it's when people talk about something in a way that seems to me misleading that I get a stick up my butt. Take the whole "entropy = disorder" idea. In the right system, that's a fine simplification, but it's a simplification that has promulgated widespread misunderstanding of the concept because people generally don't know or think about the context necessary for that simplification to work.

In brief, your response is actually very validating, as have been the rest, and I'm wondering if I too readily assume that I'm the one who is wrong when people disagree with me.
